Seminar Title:

Representation of Hydrographic Features in the Tropical Indian Ocean using CMIP6 Models

Seminar Type:

Synopsis Seminar

Department:

Earth and Atmospheric Sciences

Speaker Name:

Bali Madhu ( Rollno : 522er1005)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

ER 303, Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences

Date and Time:

14 Oct 2026 16:30

Contact:

Naresh Krishna Vissa

Abstract:

Understanding of hydrographic features using Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP) and Ocean Model Intercomparison Project phase 2 (OMIP2) models from the CMIP6 is very limited in the Tropical Indian Ocean (TIO). Therefore, the present study addresses model biases and their origins of hydrographic features against observations in the TIO. The first chapter provides an introduction, a literature review, research gaps, motivation, and objectives. The second chapter addressed the biases and their origins in models. Results showed that many models from both CMIP and OMIP2 exhibited cold temperature biases at the surface and warm biases in the subsurface. Also, saltier biases were identified in the south-eastern Arabian Sea (AS) and western Bay of Bengal. Brunt-V&aumlis&aumll&auml frequency revealed weaker stratification from surface to 100 m with a peak at 80 m. Further, vertical shear of horizontal currents revealed strong shear bias at the top 40 m, that can result in vertical mixing, which is chiefly accountable for the biases of temperatures and salinities. The third chapter analysed heat and salt transport across different straits, indicating positive transport to the north (east) and negative transport to the south (west). Positive transport occurred during post-monsoon season, while negative transport occurred during other seasons. The fourth chapter concentrates on vertical mixing, using a fine-scale parameterization to explain it through vertical diffusivity in models against observations. Results revealed that enhanced diffusivity is found within the upper 200 m in observations and models, and both ensembles underestimate its magnitude, with OMIP2 showing a lower inter-model spread than CMIP6. Further, Seasonal meridional overturning circulation (MOC) analysis reveals a strong southward overturning extending to 500 m during boreal summer, with the largest amplitude in the AS. The fifth chapter focuses on future projections using bias-corrected products. The Quantile Delta Mapping (QDM) approach was first validated over an independent pseudo-future period (2000-2014), which showed a noticeable reduction in spatial bias. Bias-corrected projections were analysed in both SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios during the near future (2031-2065) and far future (2066-2100). During the far future, basin-averaged surface temperature exceeds 27 &degC. Ultimately, QDM provides a robust framework for reducing model biases and improving confidence in future hydrographic projections over the TIO. Overall, the current study summarizes the improvements and necessity of both coupled CMIP and uncoupled OMIP2 models to accurately depict vertical hydrodynamic conditions for skillful seasonal forecasts.
